analysis.one_liner: Automatically strips endangered-species protections from any species after five years on the list.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it died in a House subcommittee, and no listed species lost federal protection.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would force the Interior Department to remove every endangered or threatened species from the protected list exactly five years after it was listed, no matter whether the species had recovered. It says
analysis.who_benefits: Developers, oil and gas companies, mining operations, timber companies, and large agricultural interests would gain, because land and water restrictions tied to a listed species would expire automatically after five years regardless of whether the species had recovered [S2][S3]. Under the current law, a species stays listed until science shows it has recovered; this bill would put a hard five-year expiration on that protection.

how_it_helps.text: Directs Interior to delist every endangered or threatened species 30 days after its fifth year on the list, regardless of recovery status.
Overrides any other provision of law, so no scientific review, public comment, or recovery criterion could keep a species listed past five years.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people would lose the Endangered Species Act's guarantee that vulnerable fish, wildlife, and plants are protected until they actually recover, and the ecosystems they depend on — clean water, pollination, fisheries — would lose that legal backstop. Species past the five-year mark would lose protection automatically [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone who relies on wildlife protection

drawbacks.text: The five-year cutoff is arbitrary: most species take far longer than five years to recover, and the bill would delist them with no scientific determination that recovery happened.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill trades a science-based protection that lasts until a species recovers for a hard five-year deadline that expires protections whether or not the species has bounced back. The benefit goes to landowners and industries facing species-driven land and water restrictions; the cost falls on wildlife and on the public interest in conservation. Most listed species need more than five years to recover, so the bill would function as a mass delisting.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to its Water, Oceans, and Wildlife subcommittee, and never moved from there before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Blaine Luetkemeyer introduced the bill on November 14, 2019, with five Republican cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources on November 14, 2019.
On December 3, 2019, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Water, Oceans, and Wildlife, where it stayed with no further action.
No markup, floor vote, or Senate action ever took place before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wildlife currently protected under the Endangered Species Act kept their protections, since no species was subject to automatic delisting. Industries hoping for a five-year expiration on species-driven land and water restrictions did not get it.

for.name: Rep. Blaine Luetkemeyer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor.

for.name: 5 of 197 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Reps. Kustoff of Tennessee, Smith of Nebraska, Rouzer, and Young).

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill; it sat in the Water, Oceans, and Wildlife subcommittee from December 2019 until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all five cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the bill died in committee without ever reaching a vote.

industries.industry: Real estate development and land use industries
industries.note: Would have gained a five-year expiration on Endangered Species Act restrictions on land development, without needing to show any species recovered. The public would lose the species protection itself.
Would have gained automatic relief from species-driven limits on drilling, mining, and access to federal land after five years, regardless of recovery.
Would have gained automatic removal of species protections that can restrict grazing, water use, and pesticide practices after five years.
Would have gained automatic removal of habitat protections that constrain logging in listed-species habitat after five years.
